subject: change of variables for compound parameter

messages.author: 3f24cff75a03e8f0
messages.subject: change of variables for compound parameter
parts:
Hi Stan folks,

This may be more of a math/probability question than a Stan question per se, but I hope that someone on the list could advise:

Let's say I have two parameters in my model, A and B, and I want the following joint prior on them:

log(A) / B ~ beta(2,2);

My question is: What is the appropriate change of variables adjustment for the compound parameter log(A)/B? This doesn't fit into the one-to-one multivariate transform situation. Right now, I am simply applying one adjustment for each parameter:

increment_log_prob(-A);
increment_log_prob(-2*B);


In the examples I have tried, this appears to get me the correct results, but I wonder if this approach will get me into trouble.

Thanks for your help,
Daniel

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] change of variables for compound parameter
parts:
The density beta(2,2) is only defined for outcomes in (0, 1).
So you'd need to ensure log(A) / B in (0, 1). Then you
run into the usual multiplicative identifiability issue, here
with a log in the middle:

log(A) / B === log(A^N) / (B/N)

If N = -1, you get sign flipping and multimodality.

This also means your transform isn't invertible (the inverse is
one to many), and thus there's no way to calculate the Jacobian.
At least I'm pretty sure that's what happens --- someone else should
check my work here, because I still count Jacobians on my fingers
and toes.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] change of variables for compound parameter
parts:
Example? If I choose something that depends on A and B and
is invertible, my choice affects the Jacobian. If I choose
a constant, I'm left with non-invertibility.

So what's going on in the original writeup is that A and
B were implicitly given priors through these statements:

increment_log_prob(-A);
increment_log_prob(-2*B);

so both implicitly get implicit distributions, as in

p(A) propto exp(-A)

- Bob

messages.author: 3f24cff75a03e8f0
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] change of variables for compound parameter
parts:
If I understand the responses correctly, I could choose my two transformed parameters to be:
  1.   log(A)/B
  2.   B

Then my Jacobian matrix is d[log(A)/B, B]/d[A,B], which has determinant 1/(A*B), so my change-of-variables adjustment is:
    increment_log_prob(-log(A) - log(B))


But, as Bob points out in his 2nd message, I could have arbitrarily chosen otherwise (here, let's say that A and B are both constrained to be positive, and n is an arbitrary nonzero real):
  1.   log(A)/B
  2.   B^n

And then my Jacobian is d[log(A)/B, B^n]/d[A,B], which has determinant n*B^(n-2)/a, so I would do:
    increment_log_prob( (n-2)*log(B) - log(A) )


I guess this can be correct: You can shift the log-prob by (any multiple of) log(B) and still end up with the quantity of interest (log(A) / B) correctly distributed, since this is just like putting different priors on the single-variable distributions... It just strikes me as a very strange result...

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] change of variables for compound parameter
parts:
See:

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobian_matrix_and_determinant#Jacobian_determinant

The point is that densities are derivatives (of cumulative
distributions) and that changing the variables affects the rate
of change. The Jacobian's there to compensate for the differential
change in volume of the transformed space compared to the original
space. The transform has to be an invertible function.

The problem here is that even if we know how log(A) / B is
distributed, we can't invert that into a distribution over A and B,
because f(A, B) = log(A) / B isn't invertible (it's many to one
as I indicated in the first message). So you might as well just
use a single parameter C instead of log(A) / B.

- Bob

> distributed, we can't invert that into a distribution over A and B,
> because f(A, B) = log(A) / B isn't invertible (it's many to one

> If you augment with the second equation as Daniel is suggesting it
> is no longer many-to-one. Major identifiability problem if you don't
> observe one of the "components", sure, but it's no longer many-to-one.

You'll have to choose the model. And then it's possible it'll do
what you want (though I still don't see why you'd want this
over-parameterization in terms of A and B in this case).

We do something similar with unit vectors. In 2D, there's really only
one degree of freedom (angle around circle). But that wraps, so is
no good for sampling near the wrap point. So instead we use 2 points
(x, y), and then project onto the unit circle. That's over-parameterized,
and if we did just that, would not be identified. So we put a unit normal
on x and y, and that identifies the scale and now everything's OK. See:

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/N-sphere#Generating_random_points

- Bob

You'll have to choose the model.  And then it's possible it'll do
what you want (though I still don't see why you'd want this
over-parameterization in terms of A and B in this case).

I've only ever used this for models where the meaningful parameters
were not identified in the final model but it was useful to visualize 
(via sampling)  how the particular model made them confounded.
This comes up a lot in ecological models with observation processes
where people observe, for example, only population counts  and mortality but they
want to model survival and immigration/emigration (http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1541-0420.2010.01465.x/abstract 
and associated elaborations).  A lot of those models are hopeless
if applied in rote fashion (i.e.-the original paper says it works, let's use
it for our data!) but they can be great if you augment the data by measurements
to resolve the non-identifiability.  Running the model (successfully) in
the original formulation is a useful way of identifying what data would
be most helpful.  

K

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/N-sphere#Generating_random_points
